packets.key_finding: A field-experiment nudge that shrouds the minimum-payment autopay option cuts minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but does not reduce credit card debt, and actually raises missed payments by discouraging autopay enrollment among liquidity-constrained cardholders.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up; JEL-coded econometric analysis of payment behavior.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry: a choice-architecture change can shift nominal enrollment/behavior metrics while leaving the real outcome (debt/savings) unchanged or worse, which is exactly the 'vanity enrollment number' risk for the round-up feature.
limitations: credit-card debt repayment context, not a savings product
no direct test of a savings round-up mechanism
liquidity constraints specific to indebted cardholders may not generalize to savers
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer self-directed financial nudge study showing enrollment/behavior change without matching real-outcome improvement, directly bearing on whether defaults would be a vanity metric here.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift investment risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes, but lower ratings of advice quality compared to no default, especially when the targeted default is refused; framing of the default question (how much to invest vs. how much to leave safe) also shifts the amount allocated to the risky option.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, in a wealth-management/investment-advice context.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern reputational risk of defaults in financial products, and shows preset framing anchors the invested/allocated amount — bearing on both the entry-mechanism and preset-level decisions.
limitations: investment risk-taking with a wealth manager, not a round-up savings multiplier specifically
experimental/survey setting rather than a live product deployment
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer-financial experiment on default framing effects on both behavior and perceived manipulation, hitting nearly every sub-criterion the brief cares about.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalation defaults are followed at the first escalation date, declining further later.
packets.methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating employee turnover, withdrawal upon separation, and auto-escalation opt-out, abstract-only for further detail.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrolment lift is real at signup and much smaller later, and preset escalation is not durably followed — a direct caution against treating opt-out enrollment counts as the success metric.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
abstract gives limited detail on mechanisms behind opt-out of escalation
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving durably, which the brief explicitly asked us to look for.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when defaults do or do not produce lasting ('downstream') behavior change, keyed to time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: Theoretical synthesis and taxonomy-building drawing on the existing default-effects literature; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a framework for predicting and measuring whether the round-up default will produce genuine lasting engagement versus a superficial enrollment bump, directly shaping what to track at 6-12 months.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, no new empirical effect sizes
general consumer behavior framework, not specific to financial savings products
packets.relevance_reason: Directly targets the brief's central question of whether default effects on enrollment persist into real downstream behavior, with a framework for measurement.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though enrolled consumers still captured less than half of available savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrollment into SMS alerts.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct evidence that a bank can auto-enroll consumers into a low-friction financial feature with measurable real-world benefit, but also that auto-enrollment alone leaves much potential benefit unrealized, cautioning against treating enrollment numbers as the full picture.
limitations: Alerts, not a savings-contribution product, so amount-saved dynamics may differ
No multi-year retention or withdrawal data reported
packets.relevance_reason: Same setting as the brief (UK consumer bank, self-directed customers) and directly tests automatic enrollment's real effect size and gap versus potential benefit.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites increased donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with the largest effects on smaller, less-experienced donors who likely did not intend recurring commitments.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences natural experiment across U.S. political campaign websites' donation checkout pages.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct real-world evidence that a pre-checked recurring-transaction default, structurally identical to auto-enrolling users into an ongoing round-up commitment, drives unintended enrollment and refund/complaint-like behavior concentrated on the least-experienced users, exactly the support team's disengagement/complaint concern.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings product, though the recurring-default mechanism directly transfers
No 6+ month retention data beyond refund requests
packets.relevance_reason: Demonstrates the mechanism the brief calls a dark default, a pre-checked recurring financial commitment, causing complaint-like behavior disproportionately among vulnerable users; the recurring-transaction default is an explicit method transfer to the round-up default question.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, all tested behavioral nudges, including default options, significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China, with default-option and positive-narrative nudges producing the largest backfire and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on pension contribution decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working assumption that defaults reliably raise enrollment/contribution, showing defaults can backfire in a self-directed savings context with highly heterogeneous effects by demographic group, exactly the caution the brief asks for.
limitations: Chinese cultural/institutional context, not EU
Online survey RCT measuring stated willingness, not real enrollment or 6-12 month persistence in an actual product
packets.relevance_reason: The explicit contradicting evidence the brief asked for: a controlled experiment where default nudges reduced rather than increased savings intent.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual from 15 months after rollout, showing active choice can durably shift users away from a preset default.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences natural experiment around EU DMA-mandated choice-screen rollout across iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: Large-scale EU-regulatory-era evidence that mandated active choice can substantially and durably overcome an incumbent default, the most directly on-point test of whether active choice captures most of the benefit of a default, in the exact regulatory environment the round-up feature will launch into (the method transfer: a forced-choice screen mandated to counteract a persistent platform default).
limitations: Mobile browser choice, not a financial savings decision
Platform-specific rollout differences complicate generalization
packets.relevance_reason: The most directly on-point evidence in this shortlist for the active-choice-vs-default comparison, in the EU regulatory context named by the brief.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: A field-experiment reminder nudge cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with the harm concentrated in users with an overdraft history who saw a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, using administrative fee data across credit card and checking accounts.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's concern that a nudge/default which helps on average can systematically harm a vulnerable subgroup, making the case for measuring heterogeneous outcomes (e.g. overdraft-prone or low-balance users) rather than just aggregate enrolment or savings lift before deciding on opt-out enrolment.
limitations: studies payment reminders rather than enrolment defaults or contribution-level anchoring
Brazilian credit/overdraft market context, not EU round-up savings
no explicit 6-12 month persistence tracking of the intervention's effect
packets.relevance_reason: Provides rigorous, consumer-financial-app RCT evidence of exactly the distributional harm-to-a-subgroup risk the brief flags as a reason not to build something that only 'works on average'.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

packets.key_finding: Field experiments show that 'active choice' (forcing a decision, no default) and a novel 'enhanced active choice' design (highlighting the losses of the non-preferred option) can motivate behavior change as an alternative to opt-out defaults, especially where automatic enrolment is infeasible or ethically fraught.
packets.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against control conditions, building explicitly on the active-choice enrolment literature (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, Metrick 2009).
packets.why_it_matters: Introduces and field-tests the exact 'active choice' entry mechanism the brief is weighing, plus an 'enhanced active choice' variant that could capture much of a default's enrolment lift without the disengagement cost of opt-out.
limitations: evidence base is medication adherence, not financial products
no measurement of contribution-level anchoring or long-run amount saved
the loss-framing nudge in enhanced active choice itself risks a manipulative/dark-pattern read
packets.relevance_reason: The key paper directly proposing and testing the active-choice design alternative named in the brief's entry decision, with an explicit note that its logic was built for savings/opt-out contexts.
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: A field-wide review of behavioral household finance summarizing empirical regularities in saving, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and cataloguing intervention types (education, peer effects, product design, disclosure, choice architecture, and price/quantity levers) used to shape household financial behavior.
alternates.methodology: Narrative literature review / NBER chapter synthesizing behavioral household-finance research; abstract gives no specific effect sizes.
alternates.why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis-level map of which choice-architecture levers work in individual financial behavior, reminding the team that product design and disclosure are viable alternatives or complements to a straight default.
limitations: broad survey chapter, not focused specifically on enrolment defaults
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
spans both employer-mediated and self-directed settings without separating the two
alternates.relevance_reason: Serves as the shortlist's synthesis/review anchor on choice architecture in individual financial behavior.
alternates.title: Behavioral Household Finance
alternates.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

alternates.key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people generally approved of financial nudges (positive on approval, benefit, ethics) except on manipulation, with stronger approval for System 2-targeting interventions framed around saving rather than spending.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment presenting 36 hypothetical financial-intervention vignettes to a representative Australian sample (n=2,100), factorially varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows which framing and mechanism choices make a financial default read as helpful rather than manipulative, directly informing how the entry flow and disclosure copy for the round-up feature should be designed to avoid a dark-pattern perception.
limitations: hypothetical vignette approval ratings, not revealed enrolment or savings behaviour
Australian sample, not the EU regulatory context
no measure of actual retention or amount saved
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly measures when a financial nudge/default is perceived as manipulative versus acceptable, the exact reputational-risk question the brief raises.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: Develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to classify when EU-regulated defaults and other choice-architecture practices constitute manipulative 'dark patterns.'
alternates.methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only, no empirical data.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete EU legal framework for judging whether an opt-out or pre-checked default in the round-up feature would read as a dark pattern, directly informing the reputational-risk assessment of the entry-design decision.
limitations: Legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence of behavioral effects
No effect sizes or outcome data
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation risk criterion central to the entry-design decision.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at all three studied firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and the conservative default fund, with half still at the default rate and fund after three years.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms over several years.
alternates.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that defaults anchor not just enrollment but the contribution level and investment choice itself — the classic evidence the preset-multiplier decision has to reckon with.
limitations: employer 401(k) plan context, pre-dating current fintech/regulatory environment
no liquid/self-directed consumer savings analogue
no discussion of active choice as an alternative
alternates.relevance_reason: The classic, heavily-cited foundational study establishing that default levels anchor participant contribution choices, which the later literature in this scan argues with.
alternates.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation while tax subsidies requiring active choice mostly shifted assets across accounts (raising total saving by only about 1 cent per dollar of subsidy); about 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' driven by automatic contributions rather than incentives.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel analysis of the Danish population's retirement and taxable savings accounts, comparing responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive automatic contribution changes.
alternates.why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that a default/automatic mechanism changes real saved amounts, not just nominal enrolment, while an active-choice mechanism mostly reshuffles assets for a minority of sophisticated actors — directly bearing on whether an opt-out round-up default would raise actual savings versus just headline enrolment.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged accounts partly administered through employers, not a discretionary consumer banking app
concerns long-horizon wealth accumulation, not weeks-to-months round-up engagement
no direct active-choice-vs-opt-out enrolment comparison
alternates.relevance_reason: Answers the brief's central question about amount saved versus nominal enrolment with large-scale causal evidence and rich heterogeneity, despite the retirement-account setting.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.
